role.name: AI Engineer
role.description: Builds, evaluates and operates machine-learning and generative-AI systems in production, including LLM applications with retrieval, tool use and safeguards, and the data and deployment pipelines around them.

researchNote: Web search and page-fetch tools were available and were used on 2026-10-01 to survey current public best-practice material: the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025), the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, public AI/GenAI engineer role descriptions and skills guides (which consistently stress Python and software engineering, LLM fundamentals, RAG, agents and tool use, evaluation, and LLMOps), scikit-learn's common-pitfalls guidance, Hugging Face PEFT documentation, MLflow documentation, published RAG practice guides (chunking, hybrid search, reranking, retrieval metrics), research summaries on LLM-as-judge biases, LLM inference-serving concepts (prefill, KV cache, continuous batching) and summaries of the EU AI Act. Only the OWASP, scikit-learn, PEFT and MLflow pages were fetched in full; the other sources were read as search-result summaries, and the primary NIST and EU AI Act texts were not opened. These were used only to decide topics and weights; every question and answer is original wording and no third-party interview-question list was copied. Not independently verified against primary legal text: the EU AI Act application dates (phased, with a proposed deferral reported in 2026) are deliberately not stated in any question, and the high-risk classification of recruitment systems was checked only against secondary summaries. Category weights are the author's judgement informed by the role descriptions, not a published standard.

questions.stem: A classifier reaches 99% accuracy on its training data but only 72% on a held-out validation set. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Underfitting: the model is too simple to capture the patterns present in the training data
A validation set that is too large, so accuracy on it is always lower than on training data
Convergence to the global optimum, so the gap between the two scores is only random noise
Overfitting: the model has memorised noise in the training set and generalises poorly
Too few input features, which always forces validation accuracy below training accuracy
questions.modelAnswer: A large gap between training and validation performance is the classic sign of overfitting, or high variance. The model has fitted quirks of the training set that do not repeat in new data. Underfitting looks different: both training and validation scores are poor. In an interview I would say my first moves are to get more or better data, simplify the model or add regularisation such as weight decay, dropout or early stopping, and reduce noisy features. I would also confirm the validation split is clean and representative, since a sloppy split can distort the gap. The size of the validation set affects the stability of the estimate, not the direction of the gap.

questions.stem: Why do practitioners keep a test set separate from the validation set when building a model?
options: The test set is used to update the model weights once the validation set has been used up
Repeated tuning on the validation set biases it, so only an untouched test set gives an honest estimate
Libraries cannot split data into three parts, so two separate sets are only a technical workaround today
The test set should be used to tune the hyperparameters, because it is the larger of the two sets
Keeping them apart makes training faster, because fewer rows have to be loaded into memory at once
questions.modelAnswer: Every time you pick a hyperparameter, feature set or model using the validation score, you leak a little information about that set into your choices, so its score becomes optimistic. The test set must stay untouched until the end so it gives an honest estimate of how the final model performs on unseen data. I would split first, tune only on training and validation data, and evaluate on the test set once. A common pitfall is peeking at the test score, changing the model and checking again, which quietly turns the test set into a second validation set. When data is small, cross-validation plus a final hold-out is the usual compromise.

questions.stem: A fraud-detection dataset has 0.5% fraudulent transactions. A model that predicts "not fraud" for everything scores 99.5% accuracy. Which approach to evaluating the model is most appropriate?
options: Keep reporting accuracy, because any score above 99% shows the model is reliable in practice
Use mean squared error, because it is the standard evaluation metric for every kind of classifier
Use training loss alone, because it is never affected by the proportions of the different classes
Use metrics focused on the rare class, such as precision, recall and the precision-recall curve
Discard most of the majority class so that accuracy becomes a meaningful measure again
questions.modelAnswer: With heavy class imbalance accuracy is almost meaningless, since a trivial model can score very high without catching a single fraud case. I would look at precision, which says how many alerts are real, and recall, which says how many frauds are caught, and plot the precision-recall curve or summarise it with average precision. Then I would choose an operating threshold from the business cost of a missed fraud versus a false alarm. A pitfall is reporting ROC-AUC alone, which can look flattering on very imbalanced data. Throwing away majority data changes the problem and rarely fixes the evaluation question.

questions.stem: Which situation is an example of data leakage?
options: Fixing a random seed so that the training and test split is reproducible between repeated runs
Fitting a feature scaler on the whole dataset before splitting it into training and test sets
Training on eighty percent of the rows and keeping the other twenty percent for evaluation
Standardising the test set with the mean and variance learned from the training set
Logging every experiment's parameters and metrics to an experiment tracking tool
questions.modelAnswer: Leakage happens when information that would not be available at prediction time influences model building or evaluation. If you fit a scaler on all rows, statistics from the test set seep into training, which makes the test score optimistic. The fix is to split first, fit every transformation, imputation and feature selection step on the training portion only, and then apply it to the test portion. Wrapping preprocessing and model in one pipeline makes this automatic, including inside cross-validation. The other options are good practice: seeded splits are reproducible and training-set statistics applied to test data are exactly the correct procedure.

questions.stem: You are building a demand-forecasting model from three years of daily sales. A colleague evaluates it with shuffled five-fold cross-validation and gets excellent scores. What is the best response?
options: Accept the scores, because shuffled cross-validation produces the most statistically independent folds
Switch to time-ordered validation, training on the past and testing on later periods
Raise the number of folds to twenty, because more folds always remove temporal bias from validation
Stratify the folds by calendar month, because stratification removes any dependency between the rows
Drop the date column, because row order stops mattering once the dates have been removed
questions.modelAnswer: Time series have temporal dependence: neighbouring days are similar, and the model will be used to predict forward. Shuffled folds put days from the future in the training set and their neighbours in the test set, so the model effectively interpolates and the score overstates real forecasting skill. I would use forward-chaining or rolling-origin validation, train on a window up to a date and test on the following period, and repeat across several origins. I would also add a gap if features use lagged windows. More folds or stratification do not remove the look-ahead problem, and removing the date column does not remove the autocorrelation hidden in other features.

questions.stem: A credit-risk classifier has a high AUC, but its predicted probabilities are used directly to set interest rates and appear systematically too confident. What is the best next step?
options: Check a reliability diagram, then calibrate with Platt scaling or isotonic regression on held-out data
Raise the decision threshold to 0.9, because that makes every predicted probability more accurate and honest
Train for more epochs, because extra training always improves the quality of probability estimates
Report only the AUC to stakeholders, because ranking quality is the same thing as probability quality
Round every probability to the nearest tenth so that the outputs look less overconfident
questions.modelAnswer: AUC measures ranking, not whether a predicted 0.8 really means eighty percent of such cases are positive. When probabilities drive money, such as pricing, calibration matters. I would plot a reliability diagram, compute a calibration error or Brier score, and then fit a calibrator, Platt scaling for a sigmoid-shaped distortion or isotonic regression when there is enough data, on a held-out set that is not the test set. I would recheck calibration per segment and after drift. Changing the threshold only changes the classification cut-off, more epochs often increases overconfidence, and rounding hides the problem rather than fixing it.

questions.stem: In a churn model, the feature "days since account closure" gives a near-perfect validation score, yet the model performs poorly in production. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: Underfitting: the model is too simple for the problem, so switch to a much deeper neural network
Class imbalance: churn is rare, so oversample the churned customers before the next training run
Target leakage: the feature is only known after the outcome, so it must be removed
Concept drift: customer behaviour has changed, so retrain the model every week from now on
Over-regularisation: the model is too constrained, so remove the penalty term from the loss
questions.modelAnswer: A feature that records something that happens after, or because of, the outcome is target leakage. A closed account obviously implies churn, so the model learns the label itself. In production that value is not available at prediction time, so performance collapses. The fix is to audit every feature for availability at the moment of prediction, usually by asking when each field is populated, and to build the training set using a point-in-time snapshot. I would then rerun validation and expect the score to drop to a realistic level. Oversampling, deeper models and retraining cadence do not address a feature that should never have been there.

questions.stem: A team tunes hyperparameters with five-fold cross-validation and then reports the best cross-validation score as the expected production performance. What is wrong with this?
options: Nothing is wrong, because cross-validation scores are unbiased estimates whatever has been tuned on them first
Five folds is too few, and a single train and test split would remove the selection bias
Cross-validation cannot be combined with a hyperparameter search in any of the common libraries
It is optimistically biased, because the winner was picked on the same folds; use nested cross-validation
The score should be taken from the worst fold, because the worst fold shows the true error
questions.modelAnswer: Choosing the best of many configurations by their cross-validation score is a form of selection bias: the winner is partly lucky on those particular folds, so its score is optimistic. For an honest estimate I would either hold out a test set that played no role in tuning, or use nested cross-validation, where an inner loop selects hyperparameters and an outer loop estimates performance. Nested cross-validation costs more compute, so for large models a simple hold-out is common. Taking the worst fold is arbitrary, and a single split is noisier rather than less biased.

questions.stem: A model trained offline with scaling and encoding done in a notebook gives different predictions in the production service, even for identical raw inputs. What is the most robust fix?
options: Retrain the model in production every hour so that the differences average out over time
Add more layers to the model so that it learns to ignore the preprocessing differences
Ship preprocessing and model together as one versioned pipeline, so both paths run identical code
Increase the batch size in the production service so that its outputs become more stable and consistent
Ask the data scientists to document the preprocessing steps on a shared wiki page
questions.modelAnswer: This is training-serving skew: the transformation logic differs between environments, so the model sees different feature values. The durable fix is to ship the fitted preprocessing together with the model as one versioned artefact, for example a pipeline object or a shared feature library, and to add a test that feeds sample raw inputs through both paths and compares outputs. Documentation alone drifts out of date, bigger models do not undo mismatched inputs, and retraining does not fix a code difference. I would also log serving-time feature distributions to catch skew early.

questions.stem: A screening model flags patients for a follow-up test. Missing a true case is far more harmful than an unnecessary follow-up. How should the decision threshold be chosen?
options: Keep the default 0.5 threshold, because it is the mathematically neutral choice for every problem
Raise the threshold until precision is perfect, because false alarms must never be allowed to occur
Pick the threshold that maximises accuracy on the training set, since that is what the model optimised
Choose the threshold at random, because thresholds do not change the value a model delivers
Lower the threshold to favour recall, using the relative cost of each error type to pick the point
questions.modelAnswer: The threshold should reflect the costs of the two error types, not a default. When a miss is much worse than a false alarm, I would accept lower precision to gain recall by lowering the threshold, using validation data and an explicit cost ratio or a required minimum recall. I would then report the resulting precision, how many extra follow-ups it creates and whether capacity can cope. Maximising training accuracy ignores both the cost asymmetry and generalisation, and demanding perfect precision would sacrifice most true cases. A threshold of 0.5 is only sensible when classes and costs are balanced.

questions.stem: A new ranking model improved offline NDCG by 3% but an A/B test shows no lift in click-through or revenue. Which investigation is the best next step?
options: Ship the model anyway, because offline metrics are always more reliable than online experiments and A/B tests
Run the A/B test indefinitely until a lift appears, however large a sample that turns out to need
Check whether offline data matches live traffic: selection bias, feedback loops and a weak proxy metric
Retrain on the offline data for many more epochs, because the model must be under-trained
Replace the offline metric with whichever alternative shows the largest improvement for this model
questions.modelAnswer: Offline and online results disagree for known reasons. Logged data was produced by the old system, so it contains selection and position bias; the offline label may be a weak proxy for the business goal; the test population or latency may differ; and a feedback loop can shift data. I would first verify the experiment itself, such as sample ratio and power, then compare the offline evaluation set with live traffic, replay with off-policy or counterfactual estimators if possible, and check whether the metric tracks what users value. Picking a new offline metric because it looks better is metric shopping, and ignoring the experiment would put a likely non-improvement into production.

questions.stem: For a regulated lending decision, a deep ensemble beats a regularised logistic regression by 1% AUC but costs forty times more to serve and is much harder to explain. What is the best approach?
options: Always deploy the highest-AUC model, because predictive performance is the only objective that really matters
Treat the simple model as the baseline; adopt the complex one only if its gain justifies the added burden
Always deploy the simplest model, because complex models are never permitted in regulated settings
Deploy both models to random halves of the applicants and never compare the outcomes of each group
Leave the choice to the infrastructure team, because model choice is purely a matter of hosting cost
questions.modelAnswer: Model selection is a trade-off across accuracy, cost, latency, maintainability, explainability and compliance, not a leaderboard. I would quantify what one point of AUC is worth in expected loss or approval quality, estimate serving and monitoring cost, and check what explanations regulators and applicants need, such as reason codes and adverse-action notices. Often a strong simple baseline with good features wins; sometimes a complex model is justified with documented explanation techniques and governance. The decision should be recorded and reviewed with risk and compliance stakeholders. Random split deployment without comparison, or a blanket rule in either direction, are both weak.

questions.stem: Why do neural networks use non-linear activation functions between layers?
options: They speed up training by reducing the number of parameters that the network has to store in memory
They make the loss function convex, so that training always reaches the global minimum
They turn every layer's output into a probability between zero and one before it is passed on
They remove the need for a loss function during the training of the network
Without them, stacked layers collapse into a single linear map and cannot model complex patterns
questions.modelAnswer: A composition of linear layers is still a linear function, however many layers you stack, so the network could only learn linear relationships. A non-linearity such as ReLU or GELU between layers lets the network approximate complicated functions. They do not reduce parameters, and they do not make the loss convex; deep network loss surfaces remain non-convex. Only certain output activations, such as softmax or sigmoid, are used to produce probabilities. In an interview I would also mention practical points, such as ReLU-style functions helping gradients flow better than saturating ones in deep networks.

questions.stem: In a transformer, what does the self-attention mechanism do?
options: It compresses the entire input into one fixed-size vector before any other processing of the sequence happens
It deletes the unimportant tokens so that the sequence becomes shorter in each successive layer
It lets each token build a context-aware representation by weighting information from other tokens
It updates the model's weights using labelled examples at the moment of inference
It splits the sequence into independent chunks whose tokens never interact with each other
questions.modelAnswer: Self-attention computes, for every token, a weighted combination of value vectors from all tokens, where the weights come from the similarity between that token's query and the other tokens' keys. This lets the representation of a word depend on its context, for example resolving what a pronoun refers to, and lets information flow directly between distant positions. It does not shorten the sequence, compress it into a single vector, or learn at inference time. Multi-head attention runs several of these in parallel so the model can track different relationships. The main cost is that comparisons grow with the square of sequence length.

questions.stem: During training the loss swings wildly and then increases steadily, instead of decreasing. Which cause should you check first?
options: A learning rate that is too low, so that the optimiser overshoots the minima it is aiming for
A learning rate that is too high, so the optimiser overshoots the minima it is aiming for
Too many training examples, which forces the loss to oscillate from one batch to the next
Too much regularisation, which always makes the loss grow steadily as training proceeds
A validation set that is too small, which changes the value of the training loss itself
questions.modelAnswer: Oscillating or diverging loss is the typical symptom of a learning rate that is too large: each update overshoots the valley and may even jump uphill. A too-low rate gives the opposite symptom, slow and steady progress. I would reduce the learning rate by a factor of ten, add a warmup and a decay schedule, and use gradient clipping if gradients are spiking. I would also check for bad data such as unscaled inputs or wrong labels. More training data does not cause divergence, and the validation set size has no effect on the training loss.

questions.stem: During mixed-precision training of a large model, the loss suddenly becomes NaN after several stable hours. Which action is the best first step?
options: Reload the last good checkpoint, then try gradient clipping, a lower learning rate and screening the batch
Delete the validation set, so that it stops producing invalid numbers during the evaluation runs
Double the learning rate to push the optimiser quickly past the unstable region and finish training sooner
Swap the loss function for a different one chosen at random and then continue the run
Ignore the NaN and carry on training, because later updates will correct the bad values
questions.modelAnswer: NaN loss means numbers overflowed, divided by zero or took the log of zero, and once weights are corrupted they cannot recover, so continuing is pointless. I would restart from the last healthy checkpoint, then look for the cause: a bad batch with extreme or NaN values, an exploding gradient, a learning rate too aggressive after warmup, or overflow in half precision. Practical mitigations are gradient clipping, a lower or better warmed-up learning rate, bf16 instead of fp16 where supported, dynamic loss scaling, and numerically stable loss implementations. Anomaly detection tooling can pinpoint the layer. Raising the learning rate would make it worse.

questions.stem: Why does a transformer need positional encodings or embeddings in addition to token embeddings?
options: Without positional data the model cannot compute a softmax over its attention scores
Positional data shrinks the model by reducing the size of the vocabulary it must store
Tokens are always shuffled during training, so positions are needed to restore the original data
Attention alone treats the input as an unordered set, so word order must be injected explicitly
Attention can only be calculated between tokens whose embeddings differ from each other
questions.modelAnswer: Self-attention is permutation-equivariant: if you shuffle the input tokens the outputs are shuffled in the same way, so the mechanism by itself has no notion of order. But order carries meaning, since a dog bites a man differs from a man bites a dog. So position is injected, through sinusoidal encodings, learned embeddings, or relative and rotary schemes that encode distances inside the attention computation. The choice affects how well the model generalises to longer contexts than seen in training. Positional information is unrelated to the softmax step, vocabulary size or data shuffling.

questions.stem: A product team wants to double a model's context from 8,000 to 16,000 tokens. Which statement about standard self-attention is correct?
options: Attention cost grows linearly with sequence length, so doubling the context simply doubles the cost
Attention cost does not depend on sequence length, because it is set only by the model width
Attention cost shrinks as the context grows, because more tokens share the same weights
Attention cost grows exponentially, so contexts longer than 4,000 tokens are impossible in practice
Attention cost grows roughly with the square of sequence length, so the rise is well above twofold
questions.modelAnswer: Standard self-attention compares every token with every other token, so the work and the attention-score memory scale with sequence length squared. Doubling the context therefore costs about four times as much in the attention layers, while other layers scale roughly linearly. Engineering techniques such as memory-efficient attention kernels, sparse or sliding-window patterns, grouped-query attention and KV-cache management reduce memory traffic or cost in practice, but long context still raises latency and cost. I would also remind the team that a longer window does not guarantee the model uses all of it well, so retrieval or trimming may still be better.

questions.stem: Why do transformer models typically use layer normalisation rather than batch normalisation?
options: Layer normalisation needs very large batches, which suits the long text sequences used in language models
It works per example, so it is independent of batch size and copes with variable-length sequences
Batch normalisation cannot be applied to matrices, only to single scalar values at a time
Layer normalisation removes the need for choosing a learning rate during the training process
Batch normalisation is patented, so open models are not permitted to use it at all
questions.modelAnswer: Batch normalisation computes statistics across the batch, which behaves poorly when batches are small, sequence lengths vary, or training and inference batch compositions differ. Layer normalisation computes statistics across the features of each individual token or example, so it is stable regardless of batch size and has identical behaviour at training and inference time. That makes it a natural fit for sequence models trained with limited per-device batch sizes. Variants such as RMSNorm simplify it further, and placement, pre-norm versus post-norm, affects training stability of deep stacks. Neither method removes the need for a learning rate.

questions.stem: You have only 2,000 labelled images and need an image classifier. Which approach is usually the most effective starting point?
options: Train a very large network from random initialisation, to avoid inheriting any pretrained bias
Duplicate the 2,000 images many times so that the model sees a much larger dataset
Fine-tune a pretrained vision backbone, training a new head first and then unfreezing layers carefully
Fit a linear model on raw pixel values, because deep models cannot work with small datasets and always overfit
Wait until about a million labelled images have been collected before starting any training
questions.modelAnswer: Transfer learning is the standard answer when labelled data is scarce. A backbone pretrained on a large dataset already encodes general visual features such as edges, textures and shapes. I would replace the classification head, train it with the backbone frozen, then unfreeze upper layers with a small learning rate, and apply realistic augmentation and early stopping, validating on a clean held-out set. I would watch for domain mismatch, for example medical images versus natural photographs. Training from scratch with 2,000 images overfits, duplication adds no new information, and raw-pixel linear models are weak for images.

questions.stem: While training a large model the loss is smooth for days, then shows occasional sudden spikes, some recovering and some not. What is the most sound plan?
options: Inspect data and optimiser state at each spike, add clipping, lower the peak rate, and skip bad batches
Increase the learning rate so that the model moves through the spikes more quickly and finishes sooner
Turn off checkpointing to save disk space, since restoring an old state would only repeat the same spikes later
Stop recording gradient norms, because spikes only appear when someone measures them
Cut the dataset to one epoch of the easiest examples and train only on those
questions.modelAnswer: Spikes at scale usually come from a combination of an aggressive learning rate, outlier batches, numerical precision limits and optimiser state such as second-moment estimates. I would first correlate spike times with data shards and gradient norms, then restore the last checkpoint before an unrecovered spike and replay with the suspect batches removed or reshuffled. Longer-term fixes include gradient clipping, a lower peak learning rate or longer warmup, epsilon tuning in Adam, normalisation placement, and higher-precision accumulation. Frequent checkpoints are essential. Raising the learning rate or stopping monitoring would hide or worsen the problem rather than diagnose it.

questions.stem: A 70-billion-parameter model cannot fit in one GPU's memory during training, even with a micro-batch of one. Which strategy addresses this?
options: Shard parameters, gradients and optimiser state across devices, as in fully sharded data parallelism
Use plain data parallelism, because every replica then needs only a fraction of the model's memory footprint
Reduce the number of training steps, because memory use is set by how many steps are run
Increase the batch size, because larger batches lower the memory held for each parameter in the optimiser
Shrink the vocabulary at random without retraining, because that frees up enough memory
questions.modelAnswer: Plain data parallelism replicates the full model on every device, so it does not help when a single copy does not fit. The memory problem comes from parameters, gradients and optimiser state, which for Adam can be several times the model size. Sharding approaches, such as ZeRO-style or fully sharded data parallelism, split those across devices and gather pieces as needed; tensor parallelism splits individual layers and pipeline parallelism splits layers across devices. I would combine them with activation checkpointing and mixed precision, and balance communication cost against memory savings. Fewer steps or larger batches do not reduce the per-parameter memory footprint.

questions.stem: In the context of large language models, what is a token?
options: A security credential that authenticates the user to the model before each request is processed
A unit of text, often a word fragment, in which context limits and pricing are counted
Exactly one whole word, whatever language the text happens to be written in
A single character, which is why languages with larger alphabets always cost more to process
A numerical score that the model assigns to the quality of its own answer
questions.modelAnswer: Models split text into tokens using a tokenizer, usually sub-word pieces: common words may be one token, rare words or code symbols several. Context-window limits, latency and API pricing are all measured in tokens, so token count is what I would budget for rather than word count. A rough rule for English is that a token is somewhat shorter than a word, but this varies by language, and non-English text or code can take noticeably more tokens. A common pitfall is assuming one word equals one token, which leads to underestimating cost and overflowing the context window.

questions.stem: What effect does increasing the sampling temperature have on a language model's output?
options: It makes the model more factually accurate, because it explores more possible answers
It enlarges the context window that is available for the model's answer
It flattens the probability distribution, so the output becomes more varied and less predictable
It sharpens the distribution, so that an identical answer is returned on every single call to the API
It lowers the number of tokens that the model is billed for on each request
questions.modelAnswer: Temperature rescales the model's token probabilities before sampling. Low values concentrate probability on the most likely tokens, giving consistent, conservative output; high values flatten the distribution, so less likely tokens are picked more often, giving more diversity and more risk of errors or incoherence. For extraction, classification and code I would use a low temperature; for brainstorming or creative copy a higher one. It does not improve factual accuracy, change the context window or the billing. Even a temperature of zero is not always perfectly deterministic in hosted systems, so tests should not depend on identical strings.

questions.stem: What does the "context window" of a language model refer to?
options: The maximum number of tokens, prompt and reply together, that the model can handle in one request
The number of past conversations that the vendor stores permanently about each individual user account
The size in gigabytes of the model weights that are loaded onto the server
The time limit in seconds after which the model stops generating its answer
The number of users who can talk to the model at exactly the same moment
questions.modelAnswer: The context window is the model's working memory for a single request: system instructions, conversation history, retrieved documents, tool results and the generated output must all fit within it. If the total exceeds the limit the request fails or older content must be dropped or summarised. It is not long-term memory, so anything outside the current request is unknown to the model unless my application supplies it again. In practice I budget tokens for each part, reserve room for the output, and remember that longer prompts raise cost and latency and may dilute attention to what matters.

questions.stem: What is a hallucination in the context of a language model?
options: A timeout that occurs when the model has to process too many tokens in a single very long request
A formatting error in which the model returns JSON that is missing a closing bracket
Fluent, confident output that is fabricated or not supported by facts or the provided sources
A deliberate refusal by the model to answer a request that it judges to be harmful
A fall in accuracy that is caused by lowering the sampling temperature too far
questions.modelAnswer: A hallucination is content that sounds plausible but is invented or unsupported, such as a non-existent citation, an incorrect statistic or an API function that does not exist. It happens because the model generates likely text rather than looking facts up. I would reduce it by grounding the model in retrieved or supplied sources, instructing it to say when it does not know, asking for citations that can be verified, using lower temperature for factual tasks, and measuring faithfulness with an evaluation set. Formatting bugs and refusals are different failure types and need different fixes.

questions.stem: A downstream service needs valid JSON that matches a fixed schema from an LLM on every call. Which design is most reliable?
options: Ask politely for JSON in the prompt, then parse whatever comes back directly without any further checks
Set the temperature very high so that the model explores many different valid formats
Increase the maximum output length so the model has room to include everything it needs
Use schema-constrained output where available, validate in code, and apply a bounded retry on failure
Wrap the parser in a try block that returns an empty object whenever any error occurs
questions.modelAnswer: Instructions alone are not a guarantee, so I combine layers: constrained decoding or a native structured-output feature that enforces the schema, a strict validator in my code, and a limited retry that feeds the validation error back, followed by a defined fallback or error path. Silent catch-and-continue hides failures and corrupts downstream data. Schema constraints guarantee syntax, not correctness of values, so semantic checks such as ranges, enumerations and cross-field rules are still needed. High temperature and longer outputs increase, not decrease, the risk of malformed results.

questions.stem: An LLM classifies support tickets into eight categories but its labels are inconsistent on borderline cases. Which prompt change is likely to help most?
options: Add a few diverse labelled examples, including borderline cases, with clear category definitions
Shorten the prompt by removing the category definitions, so that the model is not confused by too much text
Tell the model that it will be penalised heavily for every mistake that it makes
Ask the model to answer in a more creative style so that it considers more options
Repeat the single instruction to be accurate five times at the end of the prompt
questions.modelAnswer: Inconsistency on edge cases usually means the task boundaries are under-specified. Clear definitions of each category, decision rules for ambiguous situations and a handful of well-chosen few-shot examples, covering typical and borderline tickets, anchor the model's behaviour. I would keep the examples diverse so it does not overfit to surface patterns, order or balance them to avoid label bias, and measure improvement on a labelled evaluation set rather than by eye. Threats, emotional appeals or repeated slogans seldom add information, and removing definitions makes the ambiguity worse. If accuracy is still insufficient, fine-tuning a small classifier may be the next step.

questions.stem: In a 60,000-token prompt, the model repeatedly ignores a critical rule placed in the middle of the prompt. What is the best remedy?
options: Move the rule deeper into an even longer prompt, so that more surrounding context makes it look important
Trim the prompt to what is relevant, put critical instructions first and restate them near the end
Lower the temperature to zero, which forces the model to read every token equally
Raise the output token limit to give the model more time to notice the rule
Split the rule into several synonyms and scatter them evenly through the whole text
questions.modelAnswer: Models often use information at the beginning and end of long contexts more reliably than information buried in the middle, and irrelevant material competes for attention. I would reduce context to what the task needs through retrieval or summarisation, put the key instructions at the top, repeat the most critical constraints close to the final question, and structure the prompt with clear sections. Then I would check with a test set that the rule is followed. Temperature does not control attention across the context, more output tokens do not help comprehension, and padding the prompt further makes the problem worse.

questions.stem: A chat application sends the same 6,000-token instruction and reference block with every request, and costs and time to first token are high. What is the best optimisation?
options: Shuffle the static content randomly on each request, so that the model treats every request as new
Move the static content to the end of the prompt, so that caching works backwards
Put the static content first and use prefix caching, so it is not reprocessed on every request
Remove the instructions entirely and rely on the model's general knowledge instead
Send each request twice and keep whichever of the two answers arrives first
questions.modelAnswer: Prefix or prompt caching reuses the computed key-value state for an identical leading part of the prompt, which cuts both prefill latency and, with many providers, cost. It only works when the repeated content forms an exact prefix, so I would place the stable system prompt, tools and reference material first and the variable user message last, and avoid inserting timestamps or request IDs at the start. I would measure cache hit rate. Shuffling or moving the static block defeats the cache, deleting the instructions changes behaviour, and duplicate requests double the cost.

questions.stem: What does nucleus (top-p) sampling do when generating the next token?
options: It always picks the single most likely token and ignores every other candidate in the distribution
It samples uniformly from the first p tokens in the vocabulary, ordered by their index
It allocates p additional tokens of memory for every new word that the model writes
It guarantees that the output is factually correct to a degree of p
It samples from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability reaches p
questions.modelAnswer: Top-p sampling sorts tokens by probability, keeps the smallest group whose combined probability is at least p, renormalises within that group and samples from it. This adapts to the situation: when the model is confident, few tokens qualify; when it is uncertain, more qualify. It cuts off the long tail of very unlikely tokens that cause odd output, while retaining diversity. Greedy decoding is what always picks the single top token. Top-p is usually tuned together with temperature, and I would change one at a time. It controls randomness, not truthfulness.

questions.stem: When is it sensible to let a model reason step by step before producing its final answer?
options: For every request, because step-by-step reasoning always improves accuracy and is entirely free
Only for one-word answers, since long reasoning harms simple lookups of facts
For multi-step tasks such as maths or planning, accepting extra cost and not trusting shown reasoning as proof
Never, because written reasoning is always a faithful account of how the model actually reached its decision
Only when the temperature is above one, since randomness is what enables reasoning
questions.modelAnswer: Giving a model room to work through intermediate steps, or using a model designed to reason, tends to help on multi-step tasks like arithmetic, logic, planning and ambiguous classification. The costs are more output tokens, higher latency and spend, so I would use it selectively and measure whether quality gains justify them; simple lookups or extraction usually do not need it. A pitfall is treating the written reasoning as a faithful explanation of the model's internal process; it may be plausible but not the true cause. I would verify final answers with checks or tests rather than trusting the narrative.

questions.stem: The model provider announces that the model version your product uses will be retired in 30 days. What is the most responsible plan?
options: Switch production to the newest model immediately, since newer models are always strictly better
Wait until the old model stops working and then fix whatever breaks afterwards
Keep the prompts unchanged and assume equal behaviour, since all models follow instructions identically
Run your regression set on candidate models, adapt prompts, shadow test, then canary with rollback
Ask users to report bad answers after the switch and fix them one at a time as they arrive
questions.modelAnswer: Models differ in formatting habits, refusal behaviour, verbosity and reasoning, so a silent swap can break parsing or tone even if average quality rises. I would pin the current version, build or refresh a regression set from production traces, evaluate candidates on quality, safety, latency and cost, tune prompts where they regress, then shadow traffic and canary a small percentage with automatic rollback criteria. I would also review the provider's migration notes and plan for future retirements by keeping the model name in configuration and evals in CI. Waiting for failure or relying on user reports exposes customers to avoidable incidents.

questions.stem: Engineers write unit tests that assert an LLM's reply equals an exact string at temperature zero, and the tests fail intermittently. What is the best response?
options: Set the temperature to a very large negative number so that the output becomes fully deterministic every time
Rerun each test repeatedly until it happens to pass, then record the pass as the result
Assert on structure, key facts or rubric scores, since hosted inference is not fully deterministic
Disable the tests, because language models cannot be tested in any meaningful way at all
Add a long pause between calls so that the model's internal state is reset each time
questions.modelAnswer: Even at temperature zero, outputs can vary through floating-point non-associativity, batching, hardware differences and silent provider updates, so exact-string assertions are brittle. I would test properties instead: output parses against a schema, required facts or entities appear, forbidden content is absent, and a semantic or rubric score exceeds a threshold, using a mix of deterministic checks and calibrated model-based judging. Where supported I would set a seed and pin versions, and I would run evals over a dataset and track pass rates statistically rather than relying on a single call. Negative temperature is not valid, and rerunning until green hides real flakiness.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)?
options: Retrain the whole model from scratch each time that a new document arrives in the knowledge store
Store every user question permanently inside the model's weights for later use
Replace the language model with a keyword search engine that returns raw files to the user
Compress the model so that it can run on a phone without any external data
Retrieve relevant documents at query time and supply them as context, grounding the answer
questions.modelAnswer: RAG separates knowledge from the model. At query time the system searches an external store, such as a vector index or search engine, selects the most relevant passages and places them in the prompt, so the model answers from supplied evidence instead of memory alone. This makes it practical to use private and frequently changing data, to cite sources and to limit hallucination, without retraining. The quality depends on retrieval: if the right passage is not retrieved the model cannot use it. I would measure retrieval and generation separately. It does not retrain the model or replace it with plain keyword search.

questions.stem: What is a text embedding?
options: A compressed archive of the original text that can be decompressed back to the exact source text
A hash value that is always different for texts that have a similar meaning
A vector of numbers capturing meaning, so that similar texts lie close together in vector space
A list of the keywords found in the text, sorted into alphabetical order
A password-protected copy of the text that is used for secure storage
questions.modelAnswer: An embedding model maps text, and sometimes images or code, to a fixed-length vector so that semantic similarity becomes geometric closeness. This is why a search for "how do I reset my login" can find a passage about "recovering account access" without sharing words. Vector search compares a query embedding with stored embeddings, typically using cosine similarity or dot product. A pitfall is assuming embeddings are interchangeable: vectors from different models live in different spaces and cannot be compared. Embeddings are also lossy, so exact identifiers and numbers may be poorly represented, which is one reason to combine them with keyword search.

questions.stem: What does cosine similarity measure between two embedding vectors?
options: The number of characters that the two source texts have in common with each other, ignoring their order
The angle between them, so it reflects similarity of direction and ignores vector length
The physical distance between the servers on which the two vectors are stored
The difference in length between the two vectors, and nothing else about them
The probability that the two texts were written by the same person or team
questions.modelAnswer: Cosine similarity is the dot product of two vectors divided by the product of their lengths, giving a value from minus one to one. A value near one means the vectors point in nearly the same direction, which for embeddings means similar meaning. Because it normalises for length, it is not affected by magnitude differences. Many embedding models produce normalised vectors, in which case cosine similarity and dot product give the same ranking. I would always check which metric the embedding model was trained for and configure the vector index to match, since a mismatch quietly reduces retrieval quality.

questions.stem: A RAG system over policy documents often retrieves chunks that start mid-paragraph and omit the heading that gives them meaning, so answers are wrong. What is the best improvement?
options: Cut every document into chunks of exactly fifty characters so that each chunk is easy and fast to embed
Embed each whole document as one single chunk, so that nothing is ever separated
Use structure-aware chunking that keeps headings with their sections, and tune using retrieval metrics
Strip all headings from the documents before indexing, to reduce noise in the text
Retrieve fifty chunks at random and let the model work out which ones matter
questions.modelAnswer: Chunks are the units the system can retrieve, so they must be self-contained enough to be understood. I would split along document structure such as sections, paragraphs and tables, attach the heading path or document title as context, and use modest overlap so facts are not cut at boundaries. Then I would test several chunk sizes against a labelled question set using recall at k and the share of answers supported by the retrieved text. Tiny fragments lose meaning, whole-document chunks dilute relevance and waste context, deleting headings removes useful signals, and random retrieval ignores relevance entirely.

questions.stem: Users search a catalogue for exact part numbers such as "XK-4471-B", but a dense-embedding-only search often returns semantically similar but wrong items. What should you do?
options: Move to a larger embedding dimension and keep using dense-only search for every query
Cut the chunk size to a single word, so that every token gets its own vector
Remove the part numbers from the index, because embeddings cannot represent them, and search by name only
Add keyword search such as BM25 and fuse its results with the vector results in a hybrid
Ask the language model to guess the part number from the description the user gave
questions.modelAnswer: Dense embeddings capture meaning but can blur rare tokens such as identifiers, codes, names and acronyms, whereas lexical methods like BM25 match them exactly. Hybrid retrieval runs both in parallel and merges the ranked lists, for instance with reciprocal rank fusion or weighted scores, then optionally reranks. This improves recall for exact-match queries without losing semantic matching. I would validate on a test set containing both kinds of query and tune weights. Higher dimensions do not fix the identifier problem, word-level chunks destroy context, and removing the identifiers throws away the very data users search for.

questions.stem: In your RAG pipeline the correct document often appears at rank 15 in retrieval, but only the top five chunks go into the prompt, so answers miss it. What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Pass all fifteen chunks to the model every time and ignore what that does to cost and context size
Reduce top-k to one chunk, so that the model cannot become confused by extra text
Replace the embedding model with a random one to shuffle the retrieved results
Tell the model in the prompt to try harder to find the right document for itself
Retrieve a wider candidate set, rerank with a cross-encoder, and pass only the best few chunks on
questions.modelAnswer: This is a precision-at-the-top problem. A common pattern is two-stage retrieval: a fast first stage, vector or hybrid, returns a generous candidate set of perhaps fifty, and a slower reranker, often a cross-encoder that reads query and passage together, reorders them so the best few reach the prompt. This improves relevance without making the prompt huge. I would measure recall at k before and after, along with the added latency and cost. Passing everything wastes tokens and can dilute attention, lowering top-k worsens recall, and prompt pleading cannot recover documents that never reached the model.

questions.stem: A knowledge base is updated daily, but the RAG assistant keeps quoting superseded policy text. What is the best remedy?
options: Fine-tune the language model each night on that day's new documents, policy changes and release notes
Re-index changed documents incrementally, retire old chunks, and keep last-updated metadata
Raise the model's temperature so that it pays less attention to older retrieved text
Tell users to ignore any answers that look as if they might be out of date
Delete the vector database every week and never rebuild it again afterwards
questions.modelAnswer: Stale answers mean the index is out of sync with the source of truth. I would trigger ingestion from document change events or on a schedule, update or delete the affected chunks by document ID and version, record effective dates and status in metadata, and filter or boost on current versions at query time. I would also monitor index freshness as a metric and test with questions whose answers changed. Nightly fine-tuning is expensive and still not a reliable way to update facts, temperature has no link to recency, and an empty database would produce no answers at all.

questions.stem: A multi-tenant RAG application must ensure users only see answers drawn from documents they are permitted to access. Where should authorisation be enforced?
options: In the prompt, by asking the model politely not to reveal any restricted documents to unauthorised users
After generation, by scanning each answer and hoping to spot any confidential content
At login only, because every logged-in user may read any document that has been indexed
At retrieval time, by filtering candidates with the user's permissions before the model sees them
Inside the embedding model, by training a separate model for every single document
questions.modelAnswer: Anything placed in the prompt can leak into the answer, so access control must happen before retrieval results are used. I would store tenant and permission metadata with each chunk, apply the user's entitlements as a filter in the vector or hybrid query, and make sure caches and logs are also scoped by tenant. Where permissions change frequently I would resolve them at query time rather than copying them into the index. Prompt instructions are not a security boundary, post-hoc scanning is unreliable, and authentication alone says who the user is, not what each document allows. Tests should include cross-tenant probing.

questions.stem: A RAG assistant gives a wrong answer. What is the best first diagnostic step?
options: Increase the temperature to see whether a different answer happens to appear on the next attempt
Rewrite the system prompt before looking at any of the retrieved data at all
Swap in a larger language model before checking anything else in the pipeline
Retrain the embedding model on the single question that happened to fail
Look at the retrieved chunks first, to separate retrieval failures from generation failures
questions.modelAnswer: RAG has two main stages that fail in different ways. If the retrieved context does not contain the answer, the fix is in ingestion, chunking, embeddings, query rewriting, filters or reranking. If it does contain the answer and the model still gets it wrong, the fix is in prompting, context ordering, context length, instructions on grounding, or the model choice. So I log the query, retrieved chunks with scores and the final prompt, and judge retrieval and generation separately, ideally with metrics such as context recall and faithfulness. Changing the model or prompt before looking at the context is guesswork.

questions.stem: Your team wants to replace the embedding model with a newer one for better quality, but the vector database already holds ten million vectors from the old model. What is the correct approach?
options: Embed new queries with the new model and search the existing index exactly as it stands
Re-embed the corpus with the new model into a fresh index, evaluate it, then cut over
Average each old and new document vector and keep using the same index afterwards
Truncate the new vectors to the old dimension and mix the two sets freely together
Keep both models and choose one at random for each incoming query as it arrives
questions.modelAnswer: Each embedding model defines its own vector space, so a query embedded with one model cannot be meaningfully compared with documents embedded by another, even if dimensions happen to match. The safe plan is to build a second index with the new model, ideally in the background, evaluate retrieval on a labelled set against the old index, and cut over with the option to roll back. Query-time code must use the same model version as the index, so I would store the model name in index metadata. Averaging, truncating or random selection produce incoherent similarity scores and silently degrade search.

questions.stem: A vector index with hundreds of millions of chunks must answer queries within tens of milliseconds. Exact nearest-neighbour search is too slow. What is the best design approach?
options: Keep exact search and add more users, so that each individual query gets faster
Use an approximate nearest-neighbour index such as HNSW or IVF, and check recall versus exact search
Cut the corpus to the 1,000 most recent chunks and ignore everything else in it
Sort all vectors alphabetically and then use binary search to locate the nearest neighbours of a query
Place the entire index inside the language model's prompt on every single request
questions.modelAnswer: At this scale exact search becomes a linear scan, so I would use approximate nearest-neighbour methods that trade a small, measurable recall loss for large speed gains: graph indexes like HNSW, or inverted-file indexes, often combined with product or scalar quantisation to cut memory. Index parameters such as graph connectivity and search breadth control the recall and latency trade-off, so I would sweep them and compare results with brute-force ground truth on a sample, then choose the cheapest setting that meets the recall target. I would also consider sharding, metadata pre-filtering effects and rebuild cost. Alphabetical sorting has no meaning for vectors.

questions.stem: Users ask questions such as "Which of our suppliers in Germany had a late delivery last quarter?", which need facts from several documents, but single-shot retrieval returns only partial evidence. What is the best design?
options: Raise the temperature so that the model fills in the missing evidence creatively
Shrink chunks to a single sentence and retrieve just one chunk for each question
Run the same retrieval again and hope that the top chunks turn out to be different
Remove the retrieval step and make the model answer entirely from its own memory
Use query decomposition or iterative retrieval, then test on multi-hop questions
questions.modelAnswer: Questions that combine several facts, or require joining across sources, often cannot be answered from one retrieval pass. I would let the system break the question into sub-questions or retrieve iteratively, using what is found at each step to form the next query, then merge evidence with citations. For structured data such as supplier records, a query against a database or a tool call may be more reliable than text retrieval. I would build a multi-hop evaluation set and watch for added latency and error compounding. Letting the model invent missing evidence is hallucination, and repeating the same retrieval returns the same chunks.

questions.stem: What is fine-tuning a pretrained model?
options: Writing a longer prompt so that the model answers in a particular style or format
Searching a vector database for similar examples at query time and adding them to the prompt
Compressing the model files so that they download more quickly onto the server
Continuing training of a pretrained model on a smaller task-specific dataset
Deleting the parts of the training data on which the model makes mistakes
questions.modelAnswer: Fine-tuning starts from a model that has already learned general patterns from large data and updates its weights using a smaller, curated dataset, so it performs better at a specific task, domain vocabulary, output format or tone. It is cheaper than training from scratch. It differs from prompting, which changes the input only, and from RAG, which supplies external information at query time. The quality of the result depends heavily on example quality and coverage, and there is a risk of overfitting or forgetting general abilities. I would always compare the fine-tuned model against a strong prompted baseline before deciding it is worth the cost.

questions.stem: What is the core idea behind LoRA (low-rank adaptation)?
options: Delete half of the layers and then train all of the remaining ones from scratch
Train the full model with a tiny learning rate on one single, carefully chosen example from the training set
Replace the model's attention mechanism with a fixed lookup table of common phrases
Freeze the base weights and train small low-rank matrices that are added to chosen layers
Encrypt the model weights so that nobody can fine-tune them any further
questions.modelAnswer: LoRA assumes the weight change needed for adaptation has low intrinsic rank. Instead of updating a large weight matrix, it keeps it frozen and learns two thin matrices whose product approximates the update, so the number of trainable parameters falls by orders of magnitude. This cuts GPU memory and storage, since an adapter may be megabytes rather than gigabytes, and the adapter can be merged into the base weights or swapped at serving time. I would mention that rank, target modules and scaling are tunable, and that quantised variants allow training on modest hardware. The trade-off is that very large distribution shifts may need more capacity than a low-rank update gives.

questions.stem: An assistant must answer questions about internal policies that change every week. Which approach is the best fit?
options: Fine-tune the model every week and rely on its updated weights as the store of the policy facts
Use retrieval over the current policy documents, keeping fine-tuning for style or format
Bake the policies into the system prompt once and never update them afterwards
Train a brand-new model from scratch each week on the latest policy documents
Switch retrieval off and ask the model to remember last week's policies instead
questions.modelAnswer: For knowledge that changes often, RAG is the better choice: updating the index is fast and cheap, answers can cite the source, and access control can be applied. Fine-tuning is better for teaching behaviour, such as tone, structured outputs, domain-specific reasoning patterns or classification boundaries, and is a weak way to inject facts that must be accurate and up to date, because the model may blur or forget them. A hybrid is common: fine-tune for how to answer, retrieve for what to say. I would weigh update frequency, need for citations, data governance and cost. Training from scratch weekly is wildly disproportionate.

questions.stem: A team fine-tuned on 50,000 examples scraped from support chats, and the model performs worse than the base model with a good prompt. What should they do first?
options: Audit for label errors, duplicates and off-topic samples, then try a smaller high-quality set
Triple the number of epochs so that the model memorises even more of the training examples it was given
Add another 500,000 unfiltered examples scraped from exactly the same kind of source
Raise the learning rate tenfold so that the patterns in the new data override the base model's behaviour
Blame the base model and stop comparing the new results against the baseline
questions.modelAnswer: Fine-tuning amplifies whatever is in the data, including noise, contradictory answers and unwanted behaviours. A smaller, clean, consistent dataset usually beats a large messy one. I would sample and review the data, deduplicate, remove personal data and low-quality replies, check that the formatting matches the intended inference format, and keep a clean held-out evaluation set. Then I would compare with the prompted baseline again. More epochs risks overfitting, adding unfiltered data adds more noise, and a higher learning rate tends to damage pretrained capabilities. Evaluation against the baseline must continue, as it tells you whether the effort pays off.

questions.stem: After fine-tuning on a narrow task, a model performs well on it but has lost much of its general ability. Which mitigation is most appropriate?
options: Train for many more epochs on only the narrow task data to strengthen what it just learned
Remove the general evaluation set, so that the regression can no longer be seen
Increase the learning rate so that the model moves further away from the base model's habits
Re-initialise the model with random weights before training the whole thing again
Mix in general data, lower the learning rate or use LoRA adapters, and test general ability
questions.modelAnswer: This is catastrophic forgetting: updating all weights on a narrow distribution can overwrite useful general knowledge. I would reduce the damage by lowering the learning rate and training fewer steps, using parameter-efficient methods that leave base weights frozen, mixing a replay portion of general or instruction data into the training set, and applying regularisation. Crucially, I would include a general-capability regression suite alongside the task metrics so forgetting is measured, not discovered by users. More epochs on narrow data worsens it, hiding the evaluation is dishonest, and random initialisation discards all pretrained value.

questions.stem: During evaluation of a fine-tuned model, you notice that many test questions are near-duplicates of training examples. What does this imply and what should you do?
options: The model is excellent, so the high score should be reported as the final result
Nothing needs to change, because duplicates actually reduce variance in the testing process
The test examples should now be added to the training data so that the model can improve further
The score is inflated by contamination; deduplicate and re-split, keeping related items together
The model size should be increased until the duplicates stop mattering to the score
questions.modelAnswer: If test items closely resemble training items, the model can succeed by recall rather than generalisation, and the metric no longer predicts real-world performance. I would run exact and fuzzy deduplication across the splits, group by source, conversation, customer or template so related items stay together on one side, and rebuild a clean test set, ideally with newly collected examples that mirror production. I would then recompute results and expect them to drop. Merging test data into training makes honest evaluation impossible, and model size is unrelated to the leak. Keeping a held-out set that nobody trains on is a basic discipline.

questions.stem: A platform serves hundreds of business customers, each wanting a model tuned to their terminology, while GPU budget is tight. Which architecture is the most sensible?
options: Fully fine-tune and host a separate copy of the whole model for every customer
Merge all customers' data into one training set, so each customer's data shapes every model they use
Use a single adapter for everyone and let the prompt say which customer is asking
Serve one shared base model with a small LoRA adapter per customer, switched at request time
Ask each customer to supply their own GPUs and install the model themselves
questions.modelAnswer: Parameter-efficient adapters give per-customer specialisation at a small fraction of the memory and storage cost of full copies, because the large base model is shared and each adapter is small. Many serving stacks can hold many adapters and apply the right one per request, enabling multi-tenant serving with good GPU utilisation. I would also keep each customer's training data isolated for confidentiality, version adapters, evaluate each against its own test set and the shared baseline, and plan for limits on concurrent adapters and cold-load latency. Full copies are costly, pooling data across customers breaks isolation and a single adapter cannot represent different customers.

questions.stem: A high-volume, narrow classification workload is too expensive on a large model. Which approach most reliably reduces cost while protecting quality?
options: Swap to the smallest available model without any testing and simply watch for complaints afterwards
Skip quality checks, because the large model's labels are always perfectly correct
Cache every answer for ever and never retrain the model again after launch
Add ever more instructions to the large model's prompt until its price drops
Distil into a smaller model: label with the large one, review a sample, test on human labels
questions.modelAnswer: Distillation uses a strong teacher to produce examples for a cheaper student that only needs to do one narrow job well. I would sample real inputs, label them with the large model, review a sample with humans to measure label quality and fix systematic errors, train the small model, and evaluate on a separate human-labelled test set, comparing accuracy, latency and cost per thousand requests. I would add monitoring for drift and a fallback route to the large model for low-confidence cases. I would also check that the teacher model's terms of use allow training on its outputs. Swapping models blindly or trusting teacher labels without verification risks silent quality loss.

questions.stem: Why do teams build a "golden" or regression dataset for an LLM application?
options: To teach the model new facts permanently while the application is running in production
To replace production monitoring, so that no live checks are required after release
To re-run representative cases after every change and catch quality regressions early
To make the application respond faster by caching the answers to the test questions
To prove that the model can never produce a wrong answer in any situation
questions.modelAnswer: LLM behaviour changes whenever a prompt, model version, retrieval setting or tool changes, and the effects are hard to see by trying a few examples by hand. A curated set of representative inputs, with expected answers or scoring criteria, gives a repeatable measure so changes can be compared before release, ideally in continuous integration. It should include typical cases, known failures from production and adversarial examples, and grow as new failure modes are found. It is not training data for runtime learning and does not replace production monitoring, because real traffic always differs. No test set can prove a model never errs.

questions.stem: In a RAG application, what does a faithfulness or groundedness metric check?
options: Whether the claims in the generated answer are supported by the retrieved context
Whether the generated answer is shorter than the context that was retrieved for it
Whether the user clicked on the answer within the first five seconds of seeing it
Whether the embedding model that was used has more than a thousand dimensions
Whether the retrieved context was originally written by a trusted and named author
questions.modelAnswer: Faithfulness measures whether what the model says can be traced to the retrieved passages, rather than invented or imported from the model's memory. It is typically computed by splitting the answer into claims and checking each against the context, by a trained checker or a carefully validated judge model. It complements relevance, which asks if the answer addresses the question, and retrieval metrics, which ask if the right context was found. A faithful answer can still be wrong if the retrieved source is wrong or irrelevant. I would track faithfulness together with context recall so I can tell whether failures originate in retrieval or generation.

questions.stem: What is the difference between offline and online evaluation of an AI feature?
options: Offline evaluation runs on a developer's laptop, while online evaluation runs on a phone
Offline evaluation applies only to classical models, while online evaluation applies only to LLMs
Offline uses fixed datasets before release; online measures real users and traffic during rollout
Offline evaluation measures only speed, while online evaluation measures only accuracy
Offline evaluation uses no data at all and relies purely on the opinion of experts
questions.modelAnswer: Offline evaluation runs the system against a fixed, labelled or rubric-scored dataset, which is fast, repeatable and safe, and is how I gate changes before release. Online evaluation observes real usage through A/B tests, canary releases, feedback signals, task completion and cost and latency metrics, which reveals what offline sets miss, such as real query distribution and user behaviour. They complement each other: offline results catch regressions cheaply, and online results confirm business impact. Neither is limited to a model type or a single metric family. A good practice is to feed online failures back into the offline set.

questions.stem: A team uses the same model that generates answers to also grade them and reports a 95% pass rate. What is the best way to increase trust in this result?
options: Validate the judge against human labels, use a different judge, and randomise answer order
Accept the figure, because a model is always an unbiased judge of its own generated outputs
Ask the judge to give higher scores, so that the dashboard looks healthier to managers
Reduce the test set to ten examples to get a cleaner-looking and more stable number
Remove the rubric so that the judge can rely entirely on its own judgement
questions.modelAnswer: Model-based judges are useful and scalable but biased: they tend to favour their own style, longer answers and the first option in pairwise comparisons, and may be lenient with confident but wrong text. I would build a sample labelled by humans, measure agreement with the judge, refine the rubric with explicit criteria and examples, use a different model family as judge or several judges, randomise or swap response order, and monitor agreement over time. Where possible I would use deterministic checks and reference answers alongside. Inflating scores or shrinking the dataset makes the metric worse, and removing the rubric increases variance.

questions.stem: How should the evaluation set for a customer-support assistant be built?
options: Use only the ten easiest questions, so that the team sees a reassuringly high score
Start from real anonymised queries and past failures, stratified by topic, plus edge cases
Generate every case with the model under test and never review any of them
Copy the model's training data and use it as the test set for evaluation
Use only questions written by the developers who built the prompt in the first place, for speed
questions.modelAnswer: An evaluation set is only useful if it resembles what the system will face. I would sample real queries, with personal data removed, label or write reference answers or rubrics with domain experts, make sure each topic, language and difficulty level is represented, and add cases from past incidents, ambiguous requests, out-of-scope questions and attempted misuse. Synthetic data can supplement coverage but should be reviewed and not be the sole source. Test data must be separate from anything used to develop prompts or train models. An all-easy or developer-authored set gives false confidence and misses the failures that matter in production.

questions.stem: A prompt change raises the average score from 80 to 82 on a 50-question evaluation set. Should the change be shipped on this evidence alone?
options: Yes, because any increase in the average score is by definition a proven improvement to ship
Yes, because small evaluation sets are always more accurate than large ones
No, because changes to a prompt can never be assessed using numbers of any kind
Only after rerunning the evaluation repeatedly until the score finally reaches 90
Not yet: the gap may be noise, so use a bigger set and paired comparison with intervals
questions.modelAnswer: With 50 items, a two-point shift is well within random variation, particularly with non-deterministic outputs and a judge that has its own noise. I would compare old and new prompts on the same items in a paired way, repeat runs where outputs are stochastic, compute confidence intervals or run a significance test, and enlarge the set if intervals overlap heavily. I would also look at slices, because an average can hide a regression on an important category, and review the actual changed outputs. Rerunning until a target is hit is p-hacking. Numbers can be used, but they must be interpreted with statistical care.

questions.stem: Before investing in new automated metrics for a poorly performing assistant, what should the team do first?
options: Buy a generic quality score and optimise it without reading any of the outputs
Wait for users to file formal complaints before looking at anything at all
Define at least fifty metrics up front so that nothing could possibly be missed
Rewrite the whole system from scratch before measuring anything about the old one
Read a sample of real failing traces and group the failure modes first
questions.modelAnswer: Error analysis grounds evaluation in reality. I would pull a few dozen to a hundred recent failures or low-rated conversations, read the full traces including retrieved context and tool calls, and group them into categories such as retrieval misses, wrong tool choice, formatting errors, outdated information or refusals. The counts show where effort pays off, and each frequent category can then get a targeted test or metric. Generic scores optimise a proxy nobody has verified, passive waiting delays learning, a flood of metrics hides signal, and a rewrite without measurement may reproduce the same failures. This habit is cheap and reveals surprises quickly.

questions.stem: A team is rolling out an AI assistant feature and wants to confirm the new version is better in production without harming users. Which approach is best?
options: Release gradually with an A/B or canary split, watch guardrail metrics, and keep a rollback
Switch all users at once and review the metrics at the end of the following financial quarter
Show the new version only to the developers who wrote it, and ask for their opinion
Compare the new version only on the examples that it was trained on
Rely on a single thumbs-up count, since it covers every dimension of quality
questions.modelAnswer: Online evaluation compares versions on live traffic while limiting blast radius. I would route a small percentage to the new version, randomise assignment, define success metrics in advance, such as task completion, resolution rate or acceptance, and guardrail metrics for safety flags, latency, cost per request and escalation rate. I would sample conversations for human review, because thumbs ratings are sparse and biased, and set rollback triggers. Expanding the percentage in stages lets problems appear early. All-at-once release and developer-only testing offer neither representative data nor safety, and training examples cannot show generalisation.
